back: A name attached to a value: `x = 5`. `=` means 'assign', not 'equals'.
`xs = [10,20,30]`; `xs[0]` is 10 (counting starts at 0); `xs[-1]` is the last item; `len(xs)` is 3.
`for x in xs:` runs the indented block once per item. `range(n)` gives 0..n-1.
`def f(a, b): return a + b` packages a recipe; `return` hands the result back.
`if cond: ... elif cond2: ... else: ...` runs exactly one branch.
A grid of numbers of one type with a fixed `shape`; created with `np.array`, `np.zeros`, `np.arange`, `np.linspace`.
A tuple with the size along each axis. A table of 3 rows and 4 columns has shape (3, 4).
`a[start:stop:step]` includes start, excludes stop. In 2D, `A[rows, cols]`, e.g. `A[:, 0]` is the first column.
`a + b`, `a * b`, `a ** 2` act element by element, with no Python loop. Much faster and shorter.
Compare shapes from the right; two sizes are compatible if equal or one is 1. The 1 is stretched.
`A.sum(axis=0)` collapses axis 0 (rows) giving one value per column; `axis=1` gives one value per row.
Re-labels the same numbers with a new shape; the total count must match. `-1` means 'work this size out'.
Read the last line first (error type), then the line number it points to. Shape errors name the shapes involved.
When something is wrong, print `x.shape` and `x.dtype` first; most NumPy bugs are shape bugs.
